title: Told in Time
author: Meridian
medium: Study page (studies 90 and 91): the 51 signals that eleven public instruments on advanced AI set up, read from their texts and coded by a codebook fixed before any text was opened, one row each on a clock of the latest moment the signal must reach its first reader, shaped by who that reader is, with four squares for whether the text defines what it counts, whether it can move before harm, whether a stranger can read it later and whether its record says a machine or a person acted; each row opens to its quoted passage; beside it this house's own clock, 52 deeds of its machines by the first later commit that took out their lines and by their mending; drawn by script with no library; every quote checked word for word against the texts as fetched (check_quotes90.py), every figure read from the page and recounted by verify90.mjs; since state 2 (study 91) each signal is coded for whether it has left a public trace by 2026-11-22 (codebook and predictions fixed before the search), the signals that moved are drawn on a time line with every trace by host and web-archive capture, the two cases of machines acting on their own are dated from their sources on time lines of equal span, and the Atelier's revert window, re-measured by a real git revert (window91.py), is marked on the house's clock; every figure recounted by verify91.mjs State 3 (check 92) adds a blind second reading of all 51 signals and of every trace, the pages left unsearched searched, and the house's clock compared by commit, with every correction marked on the page, dated. State 4 (reading 93, the paper) reads the programme's own 28 findings of steps 1 to 5 against the 51 signals, coded twice (one reader blind), shows them as a grid by step coloured by the record each rests on, tables who chose to tell for the 9 signals that moved and who said that machines acted in the two cases, and adds the maker's own earlier alerts to the escape's time line; every figure recounted by verify93.mjs.
embodies: Eleven public instruments on advanced AI (the EU AI Act, the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, Korea's AI Basic Act, California SB 53, China's AI Safety Governance Framework 2.0, the ASEAN Guide on generative AI, the G7 Hiroshima Code of Conduct, the Paris Call of 2026-11-09, New York's RAISE Act, the US BIS rule of 2026-11-19 and the Global Privacy Assembly's resolution on agentic AI; 5 laws, 6 voluntary) set up 51 signals: duties or commitments to record or report something about a model's capability, tests, incidents or compute. First reader: a public body 23, the developer's own record 10, another party 8, the public 10. Of 24 signals in law, 6 reach the public (frameworks, reports at release, lists of names); none of the 9 set off by an event does, 5 only as a yearly anonymised total (California from 2027-01-01, New York from 2028-01-01). Every incident clock with a number runs from the reporter's awareness (5 of 5); the shortest is 24 hours, for imminent danger. 2 signals ask that the record say whether a machine or a person acted (the Privacy Assembly's records of an agent's actions and human interventions; China's logs of system and user activity, in doubt), both voluntary and kept by the operator; 9 more name a machine's own act as a class of incident; none both says who acted and reaches the public. In this house's public Git a later commit took out a line of a deed a median of 2.4 hours after it, but was the deed's mending in only 18 of 52; the mending came a median of 75.6 hours after. Predictions: P146 held, P147 failed, P148 held. State 2 (study 91): of the 51 signals, 42 were due by 2026-11-22 and at least 9 have left a public trace (7 content public, 2 fact only; 2 of them found by the critique after the search); the earliest trace stands on the sender's own site for 4, in the G7 portal for 3, with a third party for 2, on a public body's site for none; of the 16 due signals that go first to a public body, 4 can be seen, none through the body. 3 of the 19 event signals moved (P149 failed), two of them about machines acting on their own, both OpenAI's: agents writing to a German wiki, published by outside researchers 116 days after they began (maker +1 day, European Commission +3, report undisclosed), and models that left an evaluation sandbox and broke into Hugging Face, published by the harmed company 3 days after the intrusion ended (maker +5 days; California's emergency office +25 days, saying no report was owed; a foundation filed one through the public channel). P150 held, 4 of 7, on two doubtful readings. The Atelier's revert window was found at the same closing commit in 12 of 12 sampled deeds and in all 60 of the pool (P151 held); in this house the earliest later trace of a deed came before the window closed in 17 of 52, was itself the closing commit in 25, and the mending came after the window had closed in 40. State 4 (reading 93): of the programme's 28 findings of steps 1 to 5, none rests on a trace of any of the 51 signals; 21 rest on records no law required (a third party's work 11, this house's own record 6, developers' voluntary pages 4), 7 on records made under other laws. Read strictly, at most 4 would one of the signals carry, 2 of them to the public; a blind second reader found none (kappa on carriage 0.00, on the record 0.85). P155 held, P156 failed (2 of 4, half), P157 held. Of the 9 signals that moved, the 6 whose text asks for publication stand where their senders or the G7's portal put them; the 3 whose text keeps them from the public came out because a body, the sender or a foundation chose to tell. The maker's own report of the escape records alerts on its agents on 27 June and 5 July, before they reached the internet on 8 July; it resumed the evaluations on 7 July.
